[[File:PrecisionOptics Achim2.jpg|thumb|Silicon sphere used in the Avogadro project being inspected by Achim Leistner.]]
'''Achim Leistner''' is an Australian [[optician]] of German origin.<ref name="Wired">{{cite magazine |last1=Keats |first1=Jonathon |title=The Search for a More Perfect Kilogram |url=https://www.wired.com/2011/09/ff-kilogram/ |magazine=Wired |volume=19 |issue=10 |access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref> During his retirement, he was asked to join the [[Avogadro project]] to craft a [[silicon]] [[sphere]] with high smoothness.<ref>Powell, Devin (1 July 2008). [https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn14229-roundest-objects-in-the-world-created.html "Roundest Objects in the World Created"]. ''[[New Scientist]]''. Retrieved 16 June 2015.</ref><ref name="Wired" />

Leistner studied optics at Optik Carl Zeiss in Jena, Germany, and in 1953 qualified as a precision optical craftsman. He moved to Australia in 1957, and worked in [[CSIRO]] on optical fabrication methods.<ref name="optica">{{cite web |title=Achim J. Leistner {{!}} Optica |url=https://www.optica.org/History/Biographies/bios/Achim_J_Leistner |website=www.optica.org |access-date=6 June 2024}}</ref>

In addition to precision instruments, Leistner uses his hands to feel for irregularities in the roundness of the sphere.<ref name="Wired" /> The research team has called his extraordinary sense of touch "atomic feeling".<ref>{{cite AV media |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b02xgf5d |series=Precision: The Measure of All Things |title=Episode 2: Mass and Moles |publisher=[[BBC Four]] |minutes=48.4 |date=4 July 2014<!--in the United Kingdom-->}}</ref> As a result the sphere is the roundest man-made object ever. If it were scaled to the size of the Earth, it would have a high point of only {{convert|2.4|m|abbr=on}} above "sea level".<!--
FOOTNOTE--><ref group="Note">The sphere shown in the photographs has an out-of-roundness value (peak to valley on the radius) of {{convert|50|nm|abbr=on}}. According to ACPO, they improved on that with an out-of-roundness of {{convert|35|nm|abbr=on}}. On the {{convert|93.6|mm|abbr=on}} diameter sphere, an out-of-roundness of {{convert|35|nm|abbr=on}} (deviation of ±{{convert|17.5|nm|abbr=on}} from the average) is a fractional roundness {{nowrap|(∆''r''/''r'') {{=}} {{val|3.7|e=-7}}}}.  Scaled to the size of Earth, this is equivalent to a maximum deviation from sea level of only {{convert|2.4|m|abbr=on}}. The roundness of that ACPO sphere is exceeded only by two of the four [[Fused quartz|fused-quartz]] gyroscope rotors flown on [[Gravity Probe B|Gravity Probe{{nbsp}}B]], which were manufactured in the late 1990s and given their final figure at the [https://hepl.stanford.edu/ W.W. Hansen Experimental Physics Lab] at [[Stanford University]]. Particularly, "Gyro 4" is recorded in the [[Guinness World Records|Guinness]] database of world records (their database, not in their book) as ''the'' world's roundest man-made object. According to a published report ([http://aa.stanford.edu/aeroastro/posters2007/Polhode_Motion.pdf 221{{nbsp}}kB PDF, here] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080227031301/http://aa.stanford.edu/aeroastro/posters2007/Polhode_Motion.pdf |date=2008-02-27 }} <!-- Indeterminate link! --><span style="margin-left:0.2em">)</span> and the GP{{nbhyph}}B public affairs coordinator at Stanford University, of the four gyroscopes onboard the probe, Gyro{{nbsp}}4 has a maximum surface undulation from a perfect sphere of {{convert|3.4|nm|abbr=on}}±{{convert|0.4|nm|abbr=on}} on the {{convert|38.1|mm|abbr=on}} diameter sphere, which is a {{nowrap|∆''r''/''r'' {{=}} {{val|1.8|e=-7}}.}} Scaled to the size of Earth, this is equivalent to a deviation the size of North America rising slowly up out of the sea (in molecular-layer terraces {{convert|11.9|cm|abbr=on}} high), reaching a maximum elevation of {{convert|1.14|m|abbr=on}}±{{convert|0.13|m|abbr=on}} in Nebraska, and then gradually sloping back down to sea level on the other side of the continent.</ref>
<!--END of  FOOTNOTE-->

== Awards and recognition ==
Leistner holds [[Academic certificate|certificates]] in precision optics, [[geometrical optics]], optical design drawing, and [[mathematics]] from Optic [[Carl Zeiss AG|Carl Zeiss]] Jena Technical College. He has served as a member of the Australian Optical Society and on international conference working committees for [[SPIE]] and the [[Optical Society of America]].<ref>[https://stanfordwho.stanford.edu/ Stanford Who’s Who: Achim Leistner]. Accessed June 11, 2013.</ref>

In 2000 he was awarded OSA's [[David Richardson Medal]], "for the development of novel optical fabrication techniques and the design improvement of optical test equipment. By refining the Teflon lap polishing technique and performing research into the mechanism of optical polishing, he has improved the quality and precision of superpolished optical surfaces, pushing the accuracy of shapes and surface roughness down to nearly atomic dimensions."<ref name="optica"/>

In 2010 he became an Honorary Fellow with the CSIRO Division of Material Science and Engineering<ref name="optica"/>
